key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% at six months but did not reduce debt, and nudged autopay enrollees chose amounts only slightly above the minimum.
methodology: Randomized field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment with 6-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Shows a nudge/default can move nominal enrollment behavior without changing the substantive outcome and that people anchor near the preset default level — the clearest empirical case for our support team's 'vanity enrollment' worry and for anchoring risk on a preset multiplier.
limitations: US credit-card debt context, not a savings product
effect measured on minimum-payment status, not enrollment into a savings feature
relevance_reason: Closest empirical evidence that a default/nudge can lift a headline metric while leaving real behavior (and disengagement/complaint risk) largely unchanged, with anchoring on the default level.

key_finding: Abstract-only overview: automatic enrollment and default investment/contribution options have short- and long-run effects on DC plan participation and engagement, including possible negative effects on active engagement.
methodology: Narrative state-of-the-art review of defined contribution plan design literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Summarizes the analogous employer literature's trade-off between enrollment lift and disengagement, but as an employer-plan overview it doesn't resolve our consumer-app question and offers no new numbers.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
no quantitative effect sizes given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Broad review of the analogous employer default literature covering most of our sub-questions, useful background but replaceable by more targeted evidence.

key_finding: Abstract-only: default enrollment raises retirement plan participation but induces low-contribution 'passivity' and account churn, and the authors recommend combining defaults with auto-escalation and reminders.
methodology: Narrative policy discussion, abstract-only, no primary data reported.
why_it_matters: Restates the passivity/engagement concern in general terms but adds no new quantitative evidence beyond stronger papers already in this set.
limitations: employer retirement setting
no data or effect sizes given
low-impact/obscure venue, zero citations
relevance_reason: Articulates the passivity concern the brief already anticipates but is redundant with stronger evidence elsewhere.

key_finding: Abstract-only: proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework explaining when and why default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
methodology: Conceptual taxonomy and theoretical review synthesizing the consumer default-effects literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the framework for predicting whether our round-up default will produce lasting engagement or early disengagement, and names the moderators (preferences, trade-off salience) we should measure post-launch — directly shapes what we track at 6-12 months.
limitations: abstract-only, no numeric effect sizes
general consumer behavior focus, not specific to savings/fintech products
relevance_reason: The synthesis review most directly organizing the brief's central persistence/downstream question, satisfying the need for a review giving structure rather than a single estimate.

key_finding: Abstract-only: default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default option causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments, including random assignment to default options, in Medicare Part D enrollment; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Warns that persistence of a default's enrollment effect does not imply the default is good for the passive chooser — a direct caution for the distributional/welfare risk of defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: health-insurance/drug-plan context, not financial savings
low-income elderly Medicare population, not our consumer app users
relevance_reason: Strong quantitative demonstration of default persistence and insensitivity to option value, relevant to the manipulation/welfare question despite the unrelated policy domain.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalated employees escalate on the first date, with more opting out later.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans accounting for job turnover, balance withdrawal on separation, and auto-escalation opt-out.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: default-driven enrollment lift shrinks dramatically once realistic attrition and opt-out dynamics are included, directly bearing on whether opt-out enrollment numbers would be vanity.
limitations: retirement (401k) plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated enrollment channel differs from a self-directed app
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably deliver large, durable saving increases, with concrete effect sizes the brief explicitly asked for.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opted out, with the default effect strongest when incentives were high and among those unaware of their enrollment status.
methodology: Nationwide policy natural experiment analyzed with linked administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Gives a clean, quantified default effect size and shows it concentrates among the uninformed — useful evidence on who a default helps versus who it merely captures nominally.
limitations: government pay-as-you-go pension system, not a self-directed consumer app
no data on amount saved or long-run persistence beyond opt-out timing
relevance_reason: Concrete effect size (23pp) plus heterogeneity by knowledge/incentives, a close comparator despite the pension domain.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's 12-month gains in participation and contributions attenuate by 36 months, with modest average savings increases but reduced inequality in savings; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers whether the default effect persists beyond initial sign-up — showing attenuation over the medium run — exactly the persistence evidence the brief asks for, even though the setting is employer retirement plans.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings feature
switching-cost estimate calibrated to a pension life-cycle model, not a mobile app
relevance_reason: Best available quantitative evidence on medium-run attenuation of default effects, directly on point for the persistence question despite the domain gap.

key_finding: Across three experiments, including a representative sample from five European countries (n=4207), default nudges shifted risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes but lowered ratings of the wealth manager's advice compared to no default, especially among those who refused the default; framing of the default presentation had smaller but significant effects on allocation.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments on investment-allocation defaults, including a large representative multi-country European experiment.
why_it_matters: EU-based evidence that a default can carry a real reputational and perceived-manipulation cost, and that how the default is framed and presented changes its effect — directly informs whether our round-up multiplier default reads as helpful or as a dark pattern.
limitations: wealth-management/investment-allocation context rather than a savings round-up feature
advice-rating outcome, not enrollment or amount saved
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation trade-off in a consumer financial-advice setting closely analogous to ours.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans (the foundational Choi/Laibson/Madrian/Metrick study).
why_it_matters: The seminal demonstration that defaults anchor both enrollment and the contribution level itself — the baseline finding that later, updated automatic-savings studies revisit — useful as the historical reference point for our anchoring question.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, no reported year (likely dated data)
predates current app/regulatory context the brief flags as different
relevance_reason: Foundational paper establishing default anchoring on enrollment and contribution level, the classic result the newer literature argues with.

key_finding: A structural model on 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost together, and adding an intermediate 15% tip option below the existing 20-30% menu captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million transactions plus a stated-preference survey to identify preferences independent of the default.
why_it_matters: Offers a transferable method for disentangling whether adherence to our preset multiplier is driven by friction versus genuine preference, and shows that adding an intermediate menu option can recover most of the welfare loss cheaply — directly relevant if we add a 3x option to the 1x/2x/5x menu.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings product
no persistence or longitudinal engagement data
relevance_reason: Provides a rigorous friction-decomposition method directly applicable to testing whether our preset multiplier menu anchors choices through inertia rather than preference.

key_finding: In an opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings program at five UK firms, at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of a short-term, liquid, withdrawable payroll-savings account rollout across five UK employers, with 12-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: The closest product analogue to our round-up feature: shows opt-in yields very low take-up but strong persistence among adopters, directly informing the opt-in-versus-opt-out engagement trade-off.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction channel — the trusted-intermediary mechanism the brief flags as non-transferable
UK employer sample, not independent consumer app users
relevance_reason: Nearest product match (short-term liquid savings, opt-in) with concrete take-up and persistence numbers bearing directly on the entry-design decision.

key_finding: Under general conditions where designer and choosers agree on the activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal; the framework extends to cases with externalities, Pigouvian fees, and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical characterization of optimal default design using asymptotic approximations, validated by numerical simulation.
why_it_matters: Provides a normative framework for justifying which multiplier level to pre-select as welfare-optimal once we commit to having a default, complementing the empirical persistence evidence.
limitations: purely theoretical model, no empirical population studied
doesn't address a specific consumer product or measurement of persistence
relevance_reason: General normative framework for optimal default-level design relevant to justifying the preset multiplier choice.

key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, arguing EU regulation of pre-selected defaults is fundamentally about protecting consumer autonomy rather than banning defaults outright.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the EU legal framework for distinguishing a helpful pre-selected default from a manipulative one, directly bearing on whether opt-out entry into round-up savings is defensible or a reputational/regulatory risk.
limitations: legal/doctrinal rather than empirical, no effect sizes
not specific to financial savings products
relevance_reason: Only paper in the batch that directly addresses when a default is a regulatorily-flagged dark pattern in the EU, which the brief names as a reputational risk.

key_finding: A 12% default contribution rate cut the opt-out fraction relative to lower defaults (25% still at default after 12 months vs. ~50% opt-out fraction at lower defaults), and low-income employees clustered heavily at the suboptimal 12% default, showing strong anchoring.
methodology: Administrative retirement-plan data plus literature review comparison; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether a higher preset level anchors contribution choices, the exact question behind picking 1x/2x/5x with one preselected — but in an employer-plan setting where the trusted-intermediary mechanism the brief flags does not transfer.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
no explicit discussion of how the employer-trust mechanism would differ in a self-directed consumer context
relevance_reason: Strongest anchoring evidence on preset contribution levels in the shortlist, but capped by employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted/unavailable ('Trant'), so no extractable finding beyond the title's claim of four large UK payroll-savings automation experiments.
methodology: Presumably multiple large-scale field experiments on payroll savings automation; abstract-only and unusable.
why_it_matters: Title suggests short-term, liquid, automated savings experiments close to the round-up use case, but without any usable content it cannot inform a decision.
limitations: abstract is missing/garbled, no data or effect sizes available
cannot verify population, design, or findings
relevance_reason: Title alone suggests high relevance to short-term automated savings, but the abstract provides no substantive evidence.

key_finding: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though consumers still captured less than half of available savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run with UK retail banks on live customer accounts.
why_it_matters: This is the closest real analogue to our decision: automatic enrollment vs. opt-in for a feature inside a consumer banking app, with real financial outcomes rather than survey intentions, and it shows defaults deliver only partial realized benefit even when they clearly move enrollment.
limitations: outcome is alert receipt/overdraft avoidance, not savings enrollment or amount saved
no explicit 6-12 month persistence breakdown given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Provides a rare consumer-banking-app, at-scale field experiment on automatic enrollment vs. opt-in with quantified financial outcomes, exactly the setting the brief is missing evidence for.

key_finding: Over 41 months, automatic pension enrollment raised average savings by £32-38/month but also raised unsecured debt by £7/month and increased mortgage balances, partially offsetting the headline savings gain.
methodology: Randomized policy roll-out of UK automatic-enrollment pensions across ~160,000 small employers, tracked longitudinally.
why_it_matters: Shows that a default which clearly increases nominal savings can be partly offset by increased borrowing elsewhere, a caution against reading enrollment or account balance alone as evidence the default 'worked'.
limitations: employer-mediated pension context rather than a self-directed consumer savings app
debt offset magnitude may not generalize to small, liquid round-up amounts
relevance_reason: Long-horizon evidence that default-driven savings gains can be partially illusory once other balance-sheet effects are counted, relevant to the amount-saved question but off the brief's consumer setting.

key_finding: Removing auto-enrollment and adding a minor application step ('ordeal') for health insurance cut enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural policy experiment analyzing removal of an auto-enrollment default in a health-insurance selection market, with a theoretical adverse-selection model.
why_it_matters: Strong warning that removing a default (or adding friction) does not fall evenly across users — it screens out exactly the people who most need the product, which matters for judging who is helped or hurt by our entry design choice.
limitations: health insurance selection market rather than a savings product
mechanism (adverse selection) is specific to insurance, not directly transferable to a savings pot
relevance_reason: Provides some of the sharpest distributional evidence in the shortlist on who is excluded when a default is removed, though in an insurance rather than savings setting.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation boxes raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also raised refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who apparently did not intend the recurring commitment.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the timing of pre-checked recurring-donation defaults across 2020 US campaign websites.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for a pre-checked recurring-contribution default: it moves nominal sign-ups a lot, but a measurable share of that is unintended and gets reversed, and the effect concentrates on inexperienced/small users — precisely the disengagement and dark-pattern risk our support team is worried about.
limitations: political donations rather than a bank savings feature
refund requests are a proxy for regret, not a direct withdrawal/abandonment measure for a savings pot
relevance_reason: Directly quantifies the backfire/regret cost of a pre-checked recurring commitment default, the same mechanism as auto-enrolling round-ups, with a distributional skew toward vulnerable users.

key_finding: Lab experiments confirm that a default raises the reservation utility for search (a reference effect) and that people who reject the default and search further tend to find better options (self-selection).
methodology: Laboratory choice experiments testing a search-theoretic model with a reference-dependent utility default.
why_it_matters: Offers a generic behavioral-economics mechanism for why defaults change outcomes, but says nothing specific about enrollment persistence, contribution-level anchoring in a financial product, or manipulation risk.
limitations: abstract, generic lab task with no financial-product framing
no measure of enrollment, contribution level, or amount saved
relevance_reason: General theoretical grounding for default effects but too far from the specific decisions to be actionable on its own.

key_finding: Mandated active-choice browser screens under the EU Digital Markets Act produced large, durable shifts in usage — Firefox usage 113% higher on iOS and 12% higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, persisting 15+ months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered EU DMA-mandated rollout of browser choice screens on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Directly answers whether forcing an active choice can produce a large, persistent shift in behavior comparable to a default — the central evidence needed to decide whether active choice captures most of the enrollment benefit without a default's disengagement risk, in an EU regulatory context.
limitations: studies default browser selection, not financial enrollment or contribution amounts
no data on whether the chosen option is actually used/engaged with beyond usage share
relevance_reason: The clearest large-scale, persistent, real-world test of active choice against defaults under EU regulation, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: A usability study of nine opt-out interface designs for privacy choice (410 participants) found that generalizable, less-disruptive schemes increased self-reported opt-out efficiency and comfort (98% not feeling disrupted for the best scheme) at a small cost to opt-out utility.
methodology: Design and usability study of a browser-extension privacy-choice interface with 410 participants; no defaults allowed by law.
why_it_matters: Shows how to design an active-choice interface that is efficient and non-disruptive when defaults are legally or reputationally off the table, a useful design pattern if active choice is chosen for round-up entry.
limitations: privacy opt-out setting, not a savings or financial contribution decision
usability/comfort measures, not enrollment or savings outcomes
relevance_reason: Offers transferable interface-design lessons for making an active-choice flow efficient rather than disruptive, relevant if active choice is selected.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-up uptake, but for outcomes requiring real effort (passing), gains appeared only among students who were already responsive to university communication, with no effect for non-responsive students.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out across two study programs.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support-team's worry: a default reliably moves the nominal sign-up number but does not reliably move the effortful downstream behavior (here, actual exam preparation) unless it targets people already inclined to engage.
limitations: university exam sign-up context, not a financial savings decision
no financial amount-saved analogue is measured
relevance_reason: Empirically dissociates nominal sign-up from effortful downstream behavior under a default, mirroring the enrollment-vs-amount-saved distinction the brief needs evidence on.

key_finding: Following a policy change that let target-date funds become the retirement-plan default, workers' equity allocation shifted markedly toward the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of US investors, 2006-2018, analyzed around the Pension Protection Act default-option change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly reshape an allocation/composition choice while leaving the contribution-level (amount) essentially untouched, evidence for the brief's question of whether defaults change amounts saved or only nominal participation/allocation.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan setting, not a consumer app
studies asset allocation default, not enrollment or round-up multiplier level
relevance_reason: Useful negative result on amount saved not changing despite a default change, though in an employer-plan asset-allocation context rather than consumer enrollment.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, default-option nudges (along with social-norm and framing nudges) significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, with default and positive-narrative nudges producing the strongest backfire, and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing behavioral nudges including default options on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the internal premise that 'defaults will lift enrolment' — here a default nudge backfires and reduces willingness to contribute, with heterogeneous effects across demographic groups, exactly the counter-evidence the brief asked us to surface before committing to opt-out.
limitations: hypothetical willingness-to-contribute survey rather than real transactions
voluntary pension saving in China, a different cultural/regulatory context than an EU consumer banking app
small sample (220 participants)
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the batch that a default can reduce rather than increase saving intentions, with explicit distributional heterogeneity.

key_finding: Australians rated financial nudges positively overall, preferring System 2 (reflective) framing and savings-framed interventions, with demographic variation in approval.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment, 2,100 Australians, 36 hypothetical financial-intervention vignettes varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial nudge is perceived as manipulative versus acceptable, informing how the round-up entry/level choice should be framed to avoid a dark-pattern reputational risk.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not actual product behavior
Australian sample, not EU
measures stated approval, not enrollment or savings outcomes
relevance_reason: Provides direct evidence on the manipulation-perception question central to the EU dark-pattern risk the brief raises.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a bank-account delivery option had no average effect on savings, but raised balances among those with no prior savings.
methodology: Field experiment offering choice of cash-transfer delivery method; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shows that giving a savings channel does not lift saving on average, cautioning against assuming any account-based feature will drive engagement.
limitations: conditional cash transfer population in a developing-country context, not a consumer banking app user
not about enrollment defaults, about delivery channel choice
relevance_reason: Tangential evidence that account access alone does not guarantee savings behavior change.

key_finding: Abstract fragment describes contribution and interest terms of an automatic-enrollment IRA with an emergency-savings feature; no clear outcome reported.
methodology: abstract-only, uninformative fragment.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant to combining round-up-style emergency savings with auto-enrollment, but the abstract gives no usable finding.
limitations: abstract does not state methodology or results
employer/government-administered IRA setting
relevance_reason: Title suggests relevance to auto-enrolled liquid savings, but content is uninformative.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most automatically enrolled employees stuck to the default contribution rate and fund even years later.
methodology: Before/after administrative data analysis of one large US corporation's 401(k) plan change.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that defaults both raise enrollment and anchor the chosen level, the pattern the round-up level-anchoring concern is modeled on, though in an employer-trust setting the brief says doesn't transfer directly.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
2001 data, predates current regulatory and liquidity context
relevance_reason: Classic default/anchoring evidence the newer consumer-app literature is responding to.

key_finding: Abstract unavailable; title indicates a comparison of savings behavior between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined-contribution plan.
methodology: abstract-only, no content available.
why_it_matters: Could bear on the enrollment-default question but nothing can be assessed from the available text.
limitations: no abstract provided
employer defined-contribution plan setting
relevance_reason: Topically on point by title only; unverifiable content limits usefulness.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority status predict both under-saving and early withdrawal from a previously mandatory pension scheme following a policy reform allowing early access.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension early-withdrawal policy reform.
why_it_matters: Shows the same distrustful, financially vulnerable people who under-save are also most likely to withdraw once given freedom, a direct warning for the disengagement/withdrawal concern the support team raised.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme context, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
Estonia-specific institutional and demographic context
relevance_reason: Distributional evidence that mistrustful and minority savers are most at risk of the exact under-save-then-withdraw pattern support worries about.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a default-enrollment vaccination policy reduced their stated booster intentions and policy approval rather than increasing them.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a hypothetical default nudge policy.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that transparency about a default can backfire and produce backlash, directly relevant to the EU dark-pattern reputational-risk question, even though the domain is vaccination not finance.
limitations: public-health/vaccination domain, not a financial product
hypothetical policy scenario rather than actual behavior
relevance_reason: Contradicts the assumption that defaults straightforwardly help once people think about them, illustrating manipulation-perception backlash risk.

key_finding: Among Millennials surveyed in 2018, auto-enrollment and employer matching were associated with higher retirement-plan participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the FINRA 2018 Millennial Investment Study survey.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the well-established employer-plan default effect without adding new mechanism or consumer-app relevance.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer banking app
correlational survey design, no causal identification
relevance_reason: Adds another confirmatory data point on employer-plan defaults, largely redundant with stronger evidence already in the portfolio.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, each $1 spent on savings subsidies raised total saving by only 1 cent, while automatic employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation because roughly 85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel analysis of the Danish population's retirement and taxable savings accounts.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that defaults change real accumulated savings, not just nominal enrollment, and that the people defaults most affect are the least financially sophisticated, central to the 'who is helped, who is hurt' question, though in an employer/government retirement setting rather than a liquid consumer product.
limitations: Danish employer- and government-administered retirement/taxable accounts, not a self-directed consumer banking app
locked, non-liquid retirement savings vehicles
relevance_reason: The strongest available evidence on whether defaults move real savings amounts and on who is passive versus active, even though the setting is employer-mediated retirement accounts.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'enhanced active choice', active choice framed to highlight losses from the non-preferred option, motivates behavior change and is proposed as a substitute for automatic enrollment where opt-out defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and an enhanced active choice variant against standard choice conditions.
why_it_matters: The most directly relevant prior work on the active-choice entry design: shows active choice can motivate behavior change without a default, and offers an 'enhanced' variant adaptable to the round-up onboarding flow.
limitations: primarily tested in medication-adherence/health settings, not financial products
abstract does not report enrollment or persistence effect sizes for the financial analogy it discusses
relevance_reason: Directly informs the entry-mechanism decision by testing active choice as an alternative to opt-out defaults, the core comparison the brief asks about.

key_finding: A broad review of household finance documents behavioral regularities in consumption, saving, borrowing, and payments, and surveys interventions, including choice architecture and product design, used to shape household financial outcomes.
methodology: Narrative review/NBER chapter synthesizing empirical and theoretical household-finance literature; abstract-only detail.
why_it_matters: Provides the broad synthesis of choice-architecture and product-design interventions in household finance the brief wants represented as a review, spanning consumer contexts beyond employer pensions.
limitations: narrative overview rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
abstract does not itself report specific default-effect magnitudes
relevance_reason: Serves as the synthesis/review anchor for the choice-architecture literature across consumer financial products that the brief explicitly wants represented.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of enrollees initially stuck with the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, and half still did after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative data analysis across three large US firms with automatic 401(k) enrollment.
why_it_matters: The canonical demonstration that defaults raise enrollment but also anchor people at the pre-set level for years, the exact anchoring risk the round-up multiplier default decision needs to guard against.
limitations: employer-administered retirement plan, not a consumer banking app
published 2001, predates current app/liquidity/regulatory context
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence for the anchoring-on-preset-levels concern, though set in an employer retirement context the brief says doesn't transfer directly.

key_finding: Randomizing default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account in Afghanistan raised participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and it made people more likely to actively choose to save afterward.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees testing default savings-account enrollment variants.
why_it_matters: Offers rare causal evidence on why defaults work and shows the effect can persist into subsequently more active saving behavior, informing whether a default would produce lasting engagement or just nominal sign-up.
limitations: salary-linked account administered through an employer, closer to the pension literature's trusted-intermediary mechanism than a self-directed banking app
Afghan salaried-worker population, very different regulatory and economic context from the EU
relevance_reason: Provides a mechanism-level account of why defaults raise participation and whether that persists, relevant by analogy to the persistence question even though administered through an employer.

key_finding: A payment-reminder nudge in a consumer credit-card/checking platform cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, comparing reminder vs. no-reminder groups on credit card late fees and checking-account overdraft fees.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' concern: a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer fintech setting produced a subgroup that was made worse off, which is exactly the risk the support team raises about defaulting everyone into round-up savings — some users may be net harmed even as average enrolment or engagement rises.
limitations: studies reminder nudges, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit card/overdraft fees rather than savings enrolment or amounts
Brazilian market, not EU consumer-protection context
abstract gives no 6-12 month persistence data
relevance_reason: Strong consumer-fintech RCT evidence of heterogeneous nudge effects, directly informing the distributional/manipulation-risk question the brief flags as essential before building.
